source.title: PluRel: Synthetic Data unlocks Scaling Laws for Relational Foundation Models
source.authors: Vignesh Kothapalli; Rishabh Ranjan; V. Hudovernik; Vijay Prakash Dwivedi; Johannes Hoffart; Carlos Guestrin; J. Leskovec

record.file_problem: None noted. The text includes the full paper, though the referenced figures are not visually present in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests power-law loss scaling and scale-related generalization in relational foundation models pretrained on synthetic relational data, extending scaling-law analysis beyond text pretraining.
record.gate_note: Included the study's own scaling, extrapolation, and RelBench generalization results. Numerical curve values and fitted exponents are not available in the supplied text; the paper refers to Figure 1. Table 1's comparisons of pretraining strategies are not results of a scaling sweep and are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps synthetic-database count N (8–1024) and pretraining tokens S (0.5B–32B) for a 12-layer Relational Transformer. It fits Kaplan-style frontier power laws, checks held-out points, and measures zero-shot transfer to RelBench. This is a new setting (relational foundation models) with direct results on whether the power-law form carries over (V5), on extrapolation (V2), on downstream scaling (V6) and on functional-form dependence (V7). Model size and compute are never varied.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that RT pretraining loss follows a power-law trend in synthetic database count and in token count, that larger and more diverse synthetic data generalizes better to unseen real databases, and that synthetic pretraining gives strong base models for continued pretraining on real data. They also state that N and S must be scaled together and that a joint power law is unsuitable. All of this concerns a single 12-layer model; joint model- and data-scaling laws are left to future work.
record.recipe_differences: This is a scaling study of relational foundation models trained on synthetic relational databases. It varies database diversity and token count rather than language-model parameter count, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss is non-monotonic when database count or token count is increased while the other is fixed; the authors report that both need to scale together for best loss. RelBench validation scaling is unfavorable at low synthetic-database counts.

fits_no_version.finding: Pretraining loss follows a power law in the number of distinct synthetic databases (data diversity), a scaling axis distinct from tokens, parameters or compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss scales as a power law with pretraining data diversity (number of distinct sources) when dataset size is not the bottleneck.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The fitted scaling-curve parameters and plotted numerical results are not available in the supplied text. The scaling analysis is for one 12-layer RT architecture and synthetic relational data; extrapolation is described only at 2× data scale. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the scaling curves.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying scaling results identified. Numerical values from Figures 1 and 4 cannot be extracted because the supplied text contains figure references and captions but not the plotted data.

untested.parts: Language models are not studied. Loss scaling with parameters or compute is not tested; there is a single 12-layer model.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude is not tested (only 2×). Extrapolation in model size or compute is not tested.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is tested.
No depth/width or shape comparison at fixed parameter count is made.
Image, video, repeated-data and fine-tuning scaling laws are not tested. Model-size scaling in the relational domain is not tested.
There is no fitted or predictive downstream curve and no analysis of downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss.
Parameter counting, schedule and fitting-method comparisons are not made. There is no comparison against other published exponents.

missing.what: Fitted parameters (A, alpha, C) for the diversity and size power laws, and predicted vs observed held-out loss at N=1024 and S=32B
missing.locator: Figure 1 (values not in the supplied text)

missing.what: Model-selection result: the best zero-shot validation metric without continued pretraining came from 1024 RDBs at 4B tokens, not the largest token count. This suggests downstream performance is non-monotonic in tokens even at the highest diversity.
missing.locator: Section 3.3 'Model selection'; Table 4 (512 RDBs/16B base gives a lower synthetic-only mean of 66.8 vs 68.5 AUROC)

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Scaling is over data axes only (diversity and tokens) for one model size, so the results bear on V5-style transfer of the power-law form rather than on the language-model claims V1 and V3. Evidence is largely qualitative in the text, and the figures with fitted values are absent. Table 1/4 comparisons of pretraining strategies are correctly excluded as scaling rows. No uncertainty is given for the scaling fits.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests a relational foundation model, not language models, and does not report scaling with parameter count or compute.
The held-out extrapolation is described as a reasonable prediction at 2× data scale, not as prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens is tested.
The study does not compare architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Tests synthetic relational-database pretraining for one RT architecture; does not test image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws generally.
Tests zero-shot RelBench performance and RelBench validation loss under synthetic-data scaling, but does not establish a general relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss.

Shows non-monotonic loss when one data axis is increased while the other is fixed. Does not compare parameter-counting methods, schedules, datasets, or fitting methods across studies, or test compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: Relational Transformer (RT)
rows.operation_detail: Swept the number of synthetic relational databases N and pretraining token count S; fit loss curves to the minimum loss over the other axis.

conditions.value: 10k held-out contexts from 100 held-out synthetic RDBs
Kaplan et al. curve-fitting procedure; N=1024 and S=32B held out

rows.measure: Mean held-out validation loss (mean of classification CrossEntropy and regression Huber loss); fitted diversity and size power-law trends
rows.value: Authors report that scaling-frontier points roughly lie on the fitted lines in log-log plots, validating the power-law hypothesis; fitted parameter values are not stated in the supplied text.
rows.note: The reported scaling variables are number of synthetic databases and token count, not model parameters or compute.
rows.check: Linking is correct. Frontier points L(N)=min_S and L(S)=min_N lie 'roughly' on the fitted lines. Fitted exponents appear only in Figure 1 and are not in the text. The scaling axes are data diversity and tokens, not parameters or compute.

rows.subject: Relational Transformer (RT)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated the fitted scaling curves on held-out data-scale points.

conditions.value: N=1024 and S=32B excluded from fitting

rows.measure: Prediction of held-out validation loss from fitted data-scaling curves
rows.value: Authors describe the extrapolated line as making a reasonable prediction at 2× the data scale; numerical predicted and observed losses are not stated in the supplied text.
rows.note: The text characterizes the extrapolation as 2× data scale, not orders of magnitude.
rows.check: The authors call the held-out N=1024, S=32B points a 'reasonable prediction at 2× the data scale'. Within that 2× range the effect is observed. Orders-of-magnitude extrapolation is not tested, so it belongs under untested rather than a 'partial' state. No numeric predicted-vs-observed gap is given. The fit uses only 6–7 frontier points.

rows.subject: Relational Transformer (RT)
rows.operation_detail: Varied database diversity while holding token count fixed, and varied token count while holding diversity fixed.

conditions.value: Different fixed S values for diversity curves and fixed N values for size curves

rows.measure: Held-out validation loss as N or S increases with the other axis fixed
rows.value: Authors report non-monotonic, U-shaped curves when increasing N at fixed S or S at fixed N; they state that both axes need to scale together for best loss.
rows.note: The paper says a joint power law of N and S is not suitable in this setting because loss is not monotonic in either axis when the other is fixed.
rows.check: U-shaped, non-monotonic loss appears when one axis grows with the other fixed: underfitting with more N, overfitting with more S. The authors state the joint additive form of Hoffmann et al. is 'not suitable' here. This bears on V7 (the functional form depends on setup) and qualifies V5 (only the frontier form transfers, not the joint form). The fixed-axis U-shape itself is a bottleneck effect that V1/V5 already exclude.

source_check.correct: V7: observed. V5: partial; fixed-axis loss curves are non-monotonic, while power-law behavior is reported for the minimized frontiers.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, Figure 1 discussion and remark following Equation 8; text lines 563–594.
source_check.problem: The single observed state fits V7 but does not describe V5's power-law effect in these fixed-axis conditions.

rows.subject: Relational Transformer (RT)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated downstream zero-shot classification on RelBench test tasks across synthetic-data scaling settings.

conditions.value: Varied synthetic RDB count and token count

rows.value: Authors report that larger numbers of synthetic RDBs coupled with larger datasets can improve overall performance; numeric scaling-curve values are not stated in the supplied text.
rows.note: This is an aggregate across the tested classification tasks; the figure's plotted values are not present in the supplied text.
rows.check: Qualitative only: 'can improve' when larger N is coupled with larger S. The text says the AUROC results show 'similar observations' to Fig 4c, which implies poor scaling at low N. No fitted or predictive downstream trend is reported. Values are in the figure only.

rows.subject: Relational Transformer (RT)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated downstream zero-shot regression on RelBench test tasks across synthetic-data scaling settings.

conditions.value: Varied synthetic RDB count and token count

rows.value: Authors report that larger numbers of synthetic RDBs coupled with larger datasets can improve overall performance; numeric scaling-curve values are not stated in the supplied text.
rows.note: This is an aggregate across the tested regression tasks; the figure's plotted values are not present in the supplied text.
rows.check: Same as r4, for mean R2. Qualitative only; no predictive fit; values are in the figure only.

rows.subject: Relational Transformer (RT)
rows.operation_detail: Measured MTP validation loss on RelBench tasks across synthetic-data scaling settings.

conditions.value: Varied synthetic RDB count and token count

rows.measure: MTP validation loss on real RelBench data
rows.value: At N in {8, 16, 32}, larger synthetic datasets are described as suboptimal, with a clear upward trend in loss. The behavior is mitigated as N increases, and benefits from increasing dataset size become evident.
rows.note: The text reports an adverse low-diversity condition and improvement as database diversity increases; numerical curve values are not stated.
rows.check: This is MTP loss on out-of-distribution real RelBench data, a transfer measure. At N in {8,16,32} the loss rises with more tokens, which is reversed for those settings. At larger N, scaling S helps, but the authors note saturation. The mixed pattern makes partial the right overall state. 'numbers_found 2/2' is meaningless because no numbers are given.

relationships.condition: RT pretraining on PluRel synthetic relational data, frontier losses L(N) and L(S)
relationships.reason: Held-out synthetic loss frontier roughly follows saturating power laws in database count and tokens (r1), and holds at a 2× held-out point (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Held-out synthetic loss frontiers roughly followed saturating power laws in database count and tokens, including at a 2× held-out point.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: RT pretraining on PluRel synthetic relational data, frontier losses L(N) and L(S)
source_check.reason: Section 3.1 reports approximate offset power laws for losses minimized over the other data axis, extending the form to relational synthetic pretraining.

relationships.condition: Joint dependence on N and S; transfer loss on real RelBench data
relationships.reason: The joint additive Chinchilla-style form does not fit because loss is U-shaped along each axis (r3). Transfer loss on real data rises with more tokens at low diversity and saturates (r6).
relationships.display_finding: U-shaped loss along both scaling axes prevented an additive Chinchilla-style fit, while real-data transfer loss rose with additional low-diversity tokens and saturated.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Joint dependence on N and S; transfer loss on real RelBench data
source_check.reason: Sections 3.1–3.2 report non-monotonic fixed-axis curves, reject the joint additive form, and describe increasing transfer loss at low diversity and eventual saturation. This qualifies extensions beyond the fitted synthetic frontiers.

relationships.condition: Held-out N=1024 and S=32B points, 2× beyond the fit range, relational setting
relationships.reason: The authors report the extrapolated fit gives a 'reasonable prediction' at 2× data scale (r2). This is a very short extrapolation with no numeric error given.
relationships.display_finding: The authors reported reasonable loss prediction at 2× data scale without quantifying prediction error.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Held-out N=1024 and S=32B points, 2× beyond the fit range, relational setting
source_check.reason: The held-out scales and 2× extrapolation are correctly reported, but V2 specifies prediction orders of magnitude beyond the fitted runs. That extrapolation range is untested here.

relationships.condition: Higher synthetic diversity (large N) scaled together with tokens
relationships.reason: Zero-shot RelBench AUROC and R2 and real-data validation loss improve when N and S grow together (r4, r5, r6). The evidence is qualitative and has no predictive fit.
relationships.display_finding: Joint increases in synthetic diversity and tokens improved zero-shot RelBench AUROC and R² and reduced real-data validation loss.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Higher synthetic diversity (large N) scaled together with tokens
source_check.reason: Section 3.2 reports improved RelBench validation loss, AUROC, and R2 when greater diversity accompanies larger datasets. Support is qualitative; no downstream predictive fit or prediction error is reported.

relationships.condition: Low diversity N in {8,16,32}; and token scaling beyond 4B at N=1024 (from text)
relationships.reason: RelBench loss trends upward with more tokens at low N (r6), and the text says the AUROC/R2 results are similar. The best downstream base model per the text was 1024 RDBs at 4B tokens, not 32B. The token-scaling part of this reason rests on the text, not on a row.
relationships.display_finding: At diversity levels of 8, 16 and 32, RelBench loss worsened with more tokens alongside similar AUROC and R² behavior; the selected downstream base model used 1024 relational databases and 4B tokens rather than 32B.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Low diversity N in {8,16,32}; and token scaling beyond 4B at N=1024 (from text)
source_check.reason: Retain the low-diversity condition: Section 3.2 explicitly reports worsening loss with more tokens and similar downstream observations. Remove the asserted general boundary beyond 4B at N=1024: Section 3.3 selects that checkpoint by the worse of two validation metrics, which does not establish that both metrics worsen throughout larger token scales.

relationships.condition: Choice of functional form in the relational data-scaling setting
relationships.reason: The authors explicitly reject the Hoffmann/Ma joint power-law form as unsuitable because loss is non-monotonic in N and S (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Loss was nonmonotonic in N and S, leading the authors to reject the Hoffmann/Ma joint power-law form.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Choice of functional form in the relational data-scaling setting
source_check.reason: Section 3.1 explicitly rejects the joint additive power-law form because fixed-axis loss curves are U-shaped. This supports functional-form dependence, while the minimized frontiers retain approximate power-law behavior.
